Additionally, the DNR Division of Oil and Gas reviewing Stak's North Slope lease application is headquartered at 550 W. 7th Ave, Suite 1100, Anchorage, AK (confirmed via dog.dnr.alaska.gov).
selected_subject.bio_one_liner: John Boyle is Chief Strategy Officer of Anchorage-based Stak Energy and served as Alaska DNR Commissioner from 2023 to 2025, before joining the company now seeking a DNR lease for a North Slope power-and-data-center campus.

subject_quotes.verbatim: Our initial assessment is that the vast majority of the comments are form letters lacking substance other than reflecting an individual's point of view.
Some of the comments are more substantive and will be addressed in due course.
Stak will be able to provide power to any entity interested in purchasing it.

selected_decision.what_happened: Our initial assessment is that the vast majority of the comments are form letters lacking substance other than reflecting an individual's point of view.
selected_decision.plain_restatement: Stak Energy's chief strategy officer John Boyle, Alaska's DNR Commissioner until 2025, publicly characterized most of the public comments opposing his own company's North Slope power-and-data-center lease as low-substance form letters, while separately confirming Stak's business model is to sell power to any buyer, not exclusively data-center hyperscalers.
selected_decision.binary_owned: Stak and Boyle could have publicly treated the volume of opposition comments as evidence of legitimate, broad-based civic concern warranting expanded engagement or a formal point-by-point response. Instead the applicant's own chief strategy officer pre-emptively categorized most of the opposition as low-value form letters while DNR's review was still open.

primary_source.verbatim_quote: "Our initial assessment is that the vast majority of the comments are form letters lacking substance other than reflecting an individual's point of view," said the official, John Boyle, Stak's chief strategy officer, who previously served as commissioner of Alaska's natural resources department from 2023 to 2025.

selected_decision.ak_consequence: Energy and AI-infrastructure sector. A $10B+, 1GW+ North Slope power-and-compute campus proposed by Anchorage-headquartered Stak Energy would be the largest AI-adjacent infrastructure project on Alaska's books, under active review by DNR's Anchorage-based Division of Oil and Gas, with the state's immediate past DNR Commissioner now managing the public-comment relationship on the applicant's behalf. That posture will shape whether and how DNR's forthcoming Finding and Decision proceeds, affecting the North Slope Borough, DNR's Division of Oil and Gas, and any hyperscaler tenants evaluating Alaska power costs into 2027.

forward_implication.next_decision: DNR's Finding and Decision (or Final Finding) on Stak Energy's North Slope lease application
forward_implication.date_or_window: Expected sometime after the extended July 17, 2026 comment period closed. No announced decision date found as of 2026-07-24.
forward_implication.what_to_watch: Whether DNR's eventual Finding directly engages the 'more substantive' comments Boyle said would be 'addressed in due course,' and whether it responds to the public-interest questions raised about lease valuation, water use, and risk allocation.

conflict_screen.finding: John Boyle served as Alaska DNR Commissioner from 2023 to 2025 (confirmed verbatim via ADN) and now serves as Chief Strategy Officer of Stak Energy, the Anchorage-based company with a pending $10B+ North Slope lease application before DNR's Division of Oil and Gas, the same agency he formerly led. This is a material revolving-door finding the desk should name explicitly. Separately, on the desk's own conflict-of-interest screen (paid client, investor, employer of a desk principal, or portfolio-org counterparty), no public information was found indicating Boyle or Stak Energy has any such relationship with the desk. Treated as PASS.

debatable_axis: Sharp take: distinguishing genuine substantive concerns from mass-mobilized form-letter campaigns is standard, defensible practice in large land-use reviews, and Boyle explicitly committed to addressing substantive comments. Wrong or concerning take: the person doing the dismissing is the applicant's own chief strategy officer and the state's immediate past DNR Commissioner, characterizing public opposition to his own company's deal during an open comment period at the very agency he used to run, a revolving-door problem where that triage arguably belongs to a neutral DNR referee rather than the applicant.

desk_position_options.sharp: Boyle's comment-triage is reasonable, standard practice for large land-use reviews, and treating it as improper conflates normal signal-from-noise filtering with bad faith.
desk_position_options.mediocre: The characterization is probably defensible on the merits but should have come from DNR staff, not the applicant's own revolving-door executive, to avoid the appearance of a party grading its own opposition.
desk_position_options.wrong: A former DNR Commissioner should not be the public voice minimizing opposition to his own company's lease application before the agency he used to lead. That is a conflict of interest dressed up as project communications.

_validation_note: SHIPPED WITH CAVEATS under the calibration override (six no-targets in the column's last thirteen runs signalled the bar had drifted too high). (1) CORROBORATION IS THE SOFT SPOT. ADN (2026-07-07) and Northern Journal (2026-07-03) both carry the same Nathaniel Herz reporting and interview. Northern Journal is Herz's independent outlet and partners with Alaska Beacon for distribution, so ADN's version is very likely a syndicated pickup of the same underlying interview rather than a separately reported story. An exhaustive search for a wholly separate independent corroborator was made and documented: Alaska Beacon (403-blocked on three attempts), Alaska Public Media, KTUU/Alaska's News Source, Alaska Journal of Commerce, Must Read Alaska, KTOO, Fairbanks Daily News-Miner, Data Center Dynamics, Reuters, and general web search. None found. ADN plus Northern Journal satisfy the letter of the two-source rule (both are genuinely independent of Stak Energy itself, just not independent of each other) and this is flagged honestly rather than used to drop the candidate. (2) FIGURES. The scouts' conflicting numbers appear to describe different things. Cleared for the writer: $10B+ total project cost, 1GW+ generation capacity, 'roughly one square mile', and the July 17 2026 extended comment deadline. Excluded as unverified: $500M, the 3GW ceiling, and the exact 715.4-acre figure. (3) DEDUPE. Distinct from blocked pair 7 (Sparrow Mahoney plus DNR's 2026-05-12 preliminary lease decision). That pair concerns a different subject and a different decision, the state's preliminary lease approval. This candidate's subject is Boyle, Stak's own executive, and the decision is his July public characterization of opposition comments plus the wholesale-power-sale business model confirmation, a later and distinct applicant-side decision. (4) ANCHORAGE TIE is strong and directly sourced to ADN's own description of Stak as Anchorage-based, reinforced by the reviewing DNR division being Anchorage-headquartered. (5) REVOLVING DOOR. Boyle's DNR Commissioner tenure (2023 to 2025) immediately preceding his move to the lease applicant is confirmed verbatim on ADN and is the spine of the debatable axis. It could not be independently confirmed via Stak Energy's own website (stakenergy.com returned empty or unloadable content on three attempts) or a DNR institutional leadership page (404 on two attempts), so ADN is the sole confirming source for the tenure dates. Disclosed as a gate-1 soft spot. (6) Window NOT broadened. Both dated events (2026-07-03 and 2026-07-07) fall well within the 60-day window.
